items.title: snick
items.text:
Handy gadgets for taming indented text

A small collection of practical utilities for working with indented strings and text formatting:

  • Dedent triple-quoted strings without giving up indented code
  • Build multi-line output line by line with Conjoiner
  • Format data structures like pprint, but with json.dumps-style indentation and trailing commas
  • Strip ANSI codes and stray whitespace from terminal output
  • Wrap and indent text blocks for logs and reports

Built on the Python standard library. Nothing extra to install.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: • Python 3.10 or greater

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Install the latest release from PyPI:

pip install snick

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
Dedent a triple-quoted string without sacrificing indented code:

dedent() example
import snick

def my_function():
    return snick.dedent(
        """
        Oops! Something went wrong.
        Here's what happened:
            - The flux capacitor overheated
            - Time circuits malfunctioned
        Please try again later.
        """
    )

print(my_function())
output
Oops! Something went wrong.
Here's what happened:
    - The flux capacitor overheated
    - Time circuits malfunctioned
Please try again later.

Build multi-line output line by line:

Conjoiner example
def generate_report(name, tasks):
    report = snick.Conjoiner()
    report.add(f"Daily Report for {name}", blanks_after=1)

    if tasks:
        report.add("Completed Tasks:")
        report.extend(f"  ✓ {task}" for task in tasks)
    else:
        report.add("No tasks completed today.")

    return str(report)

print(generate_report("Alice", ["Fix bug #123", "Review PR #456", "Deploy v2.0"]))
output
Daily Report for Alice

Completed Tasks:
  ✓ Fix bug #123
  ✓ Review PR #456
  ✓ Deploy v2.0

Format a data structure with consistent indentation:

pretty_format() example
data = {
    'user': 'bob',
    'permissions': ['read', 'write', 'execute'],
    'metadata': {'created': '2026-01-22', 'active': True}
}
print(snick.pretty_format(data))
output
{
  'user': 'bob',
  'permissions': [
    'read',
    'write',
    'execute',
  ],
  'metadata': {
    'created': '2026-01-22',
    'active': True,
  },
}

For more examples, see the Features page.

See it in action

The fastest way to get a feel for snick is to run the interactive demo:

uvx --from=snick[demo] snick-demo

No install required. See the Demo page for a full overview of what it covers.

Prefer reading code? The examples/ directory has a standalone script for every feature.

items.title: What's with the name?
items.text: There aren't many good synonyms for the verb "indent", but there are a few for the act of making a small dent in something. "Snick" means "to cut a small notch or incision in." Close enough.

items.title: Demo
items.text: snick ships with an interactive demo that walks through every feature, one function at a time. It's the quickest way to see what the library can do before writing any code of your own.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
The demo depends on typer, rich, and auto-name-enum, which aren't pulled in by a plain snick install. Add them with the demo extra:

uv add snick[demo]

To try it without touching your current environment:

uvx --from=snick[demo] snick-demo

items.title: Running the demo
items.text:
snick-demo

The demo opens with a feature listing and asks whether to continue. Each step shows the source code and the captured output, then prompts you to move on.

Feature What it covers conjoin Joining strings with a configurable separator conjoiner Building multi-line output incrementally with Conjoiner dedent Stripping common indentation from triple-quoted strings dedent_all Dedenting multiple blobs and joining them enboxify Drawing an ASCII box around a block of text indent Adding a prefix to every line unwrap Collapsing a wrapped paragraph into a single line strip Removing whitespace and ANSI escape sequences pretty Rendering nested data structures with clean indentation

To jump straight to one feature, pass --feature:

snick-demo --feature=conjoiner

For the full list of options:

snick-demo --help

Browse it on GitHub

items.title: Features
items.text: snick provides a set of text manipulation functions and a Conjoiner class for building multi-line strings incrementally. All functions accept additional keyword arguments to customize their behavior.

items.title: dedent()
items.text: Unindents a block of text by aligning all lines with the leftmost non-whitespace character. Useful for triple-quoted strings inside indented code.

items.title: Example
items.text:
dedent() example
import snick

class Whatever:
    @staticmethod
    def print_some_stuff():
        print(
            snick.dedent(
                """
                Here is some text
                    here is some other text
                    we don't want this indented
                    when it's printed
                      (to the console)
                """
            )
        )
output
Here is some text
    here is some other text
    we don't want this indented
    when it's printed
      (to the console)

items.title: should_strip (bool)
items.text:
If False, should_strip preserves leading and trailing newlines. Default is True.

dedent() with should_strip=False
dummy_text = """
    Here is some text
        here is some other text
"""
print(snick.dedent(dummy_text, should_strip=False))
output (with blank lines preserved)
Here is some text
    here is some other text

items.title: indent()
items.text: Indents a block of text. This is a thin wrapper around textwrap.indent() with sensible defaults.

items.title: Example
items.text:
indent() example
lines = [
    "would be so nice",
    "to indent these",
    "i guess",
]
print(snick.indent("\n".join(lines)))
output
    would be so nice
    to indent these
    i guess

items.title: prefix (str)
items.text:
The string to prepend to each line. Default is " " (4 spaces).

indent() with prefix
lines = [
    "would be so nice",
    "to indent these",
    "i guess",
]
print(snick.indent("\n".join(lines), prefix=">> "))
output
>> would be so nice
>> to indent these
>> i guess

items.title: predicate (callable)
items.text:
A function that determines which lines to indent. Only lines for which it returns True are prefixed.

indent() with predicate
lines = [
    "would be so nice",
    "to indent these",
    "i guess",
]
print(snick.indent("\n".join(lines), predicate=lambda line: "indent" in line))
output
would be so nice
    to indent these
i guess

items.title: skip_first_line (bool)
items.text:
If True, the first line is not indented. Default is False.

indent() with skip_first_line
lines = [
    "do not indent me",
    "indent me, though",
    "and me",
]
print(snick.indent("\n".join(lines)), skip_first_line=True))
output
do not indent me
    indent me, though
    and me

items.title: dedent_all()
items.text: Applies dedent() to each argument separately and joins them together (using conjoin().

items.title: Example
items.text:
dedent_all() example
print(
    snick.dedent_all(
        """
        Here is a long bit of text
        as an introduction to the
        following dynamic items:
        --------------------------
        """,
        *(f"* Item #{i}" for i in range(1, 4)),
    )
)
output
Here is a long bit of text
as an introduction to the
following dynamic items:
--------------------------
* Item #1
* Item #2
* Item #3

items.title: should_strip (bool)
items.text: Passed through to each dedent() call. See dedent().

items.title: join_str (str)
items.text: The string used to join the dedented parts. See conjoin().

items.title: unwrap()
items.text: Joins all lines in a block of text into a single string. Useful for long strings in deeply indented code.

items.title: Example
should_strip (bool)
items.text: Passed through to the internal dedent() call. See dedent().

items.title: separator (str)
items.text:
The string used to join lines after dedenting. Default is " " (a single space).

unwrap() with separator
print(
    snick.unwrap(
        """
        These lines
        need to be joined
        with a custom separator
        """,
        separator=" / ",
    )
)
output
These lines / need to be joined / with a custom separator

items.title: conjoin()
items.text: Like Python's built-in join(), but accepts items as arguments instead of requiring an iterable.

items.title: Example
items.text:
conjoin() example
print(
    snick.conjoin(
        "Here are some lines",
        "that I would like to join",
        "and it would be silly",
        "to have to wrap them in a",
        "list instead of just passing",
        "them as plain old arguments",
    )
)
output
Here are some lines
that I would like to join
and it would be silly
to have to wrap them in a
list instead of just passing
them as plain old arguments

items.title: join_str (str)
items.text:
The string used to join the arguments. Default is "\n".

conjoin() with join_str
print(
    snick.conjoin(
        "These lines",
        "need to be joined",
        "with a custom separator",
        join_str=" / ",
    )
)
output
These lines / need to be joined / with a custom separator

items.title: strip_whitespace()
items.text: Removes all whitespace from a string, including newlines, tabs, and spaces. Handy for tests.

items.title: Example
items.text:
strip_whitespace() example
print(
    snick.strip_whitespace(
        """
        some text with    whitespace
        and whatnot
        """
    )
)
output
sometextwithwhitespaceandwhatnot

items.title: strip_trailing_whitespace()
items.text: Removes trailing whitespace from each line in a multi-line string.

items.title: Example
items.text:
strip_trailing_whitespace() example
print(snick.strip_trailing_whitespace(
    snick.conjoin(
        "  here is a string with a bundle of    ",
        "  trailing whitespace. ",
        "  we want it all gone.                    ",
    )
))
output
  here is a string with a bundle of
  trailing whitespace.
  we want it all gone.

items.title: strip_ansi_escape_sequences()
items.text: Removes ANSI escape sequences from text, such as those added by terminal applications for color and formatting.

items.title: Example
items.text:
strip_ansi_escape_sequences() example
print(
    snick.strip_ansi_escape_sequences(
        snick.dedent(
            """
            \033[31mhere's some text\033[0m with
            \033[32mansi control codes\033[0m added
            \033[33mincluding a few\033[0m
            \033[34mdifferent colors\033[0m
            \033[1mand bold text\033[0m.
            """
        )
    )
)
output
here's some text with
ansi control codes added
including a few
different colors
and bold text.

items.title: indent_wrap()
items.text: Wraps a long string and indents each wrapped line.

items.title: Example
items.text:
indent_wrap() example
long_text = "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua."
print("Here's some filler text:")
print(snick.indent_wrap(long_text, width=70, indent=4))
output
Here's some filler text:
    Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do
    eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.

items.title: Parameters
items.text: All keyword arguments are passed through to textwrap.fill(). The most commonly useful ones are:

items.title: width (int)
items.text: The maximum line width. Default is 80.

items.title: indent (int)
items.text: Number of spaces to prefix each line with. Passed to textwrap.fill() as initial_indent. Default is 4.

items.title: subsequent_indent (str)
items.text: The prefix applied to all lines after the first. indent_wrap sets this automatically to match any leading whitespace on the input text, but you can override it explicitly.

items.title: break_long_words (bool)
items.text: If True, words longer than width are broken across lines. Default is True.

items.title: break_on_hyphens (bool)
items.text: If True, wrapping may occur on hyphens in compound words. Default is True.

items.title: pretty_format()
items.text: Formats Python data structures (dict, list, tuple, or combinations) with consistent indentation and trailing commas, similar to json.dumps(indent=2) but for arbitrary Python objects.

items.title: Example
indent (int)
items.text: Number of spaces per indentation level. Default is 2.

items.title: pretty_print()
items.text: Same as pretty_format() but prints to a stream instead of returning a string.

items.title: Example
items.text:
pretty_print() example
snick.pretty_print(data)  # prints to stdout

items.title: stream (file-like)
items.text:
The output stream to print to. Default is sys.stdout.

pretty_print() with stream
import sys

data = {
    "name": "example",
    "values": [1, 2, 3],
}
snick.pretty_print(data, stream=sys.stderr)

items.title: indent (int)
items.text:
Number of spaces per indentation level. Default is 2.

pretty_print() with indent
data = {
    "name": "example",
    "values": [1, 2, 3],
}
snick.pretty_print(data, indent=4)
output
{
    'name': 'example',
    'values': [
        1,
        2,
        3,
    ],
}

items.title: enboxify()
items.text: Draws a box around a block of text.

items.title: Example
items.text:
enboxify() example
print(
    snick.enboxify(
        """
        here's some text that we
        want to put into a box.
        That will make it look
        so very nice
        """
    )
)
output
****************************
* here's some text that we *
* want to put into a box.  *
* That will make it look   *
* so very nice             *
****************************

items.title: boxchar (str)
items.text:
The single character used to draw the box. Default is "*".

enboxify() with boxchar
print(
    snick.enboxify(
        """
        here's some text that we
        want to put into a box.
        """,
        boxchar="#",
    )
)
output
############################
# here's some text that we #
# want to put into a box.  #
############################

items.title: hspace (int)
items.text:
Number of spaces between the text and the box on the left and right. Default is 1.

enboxify() with hspace
print(
    snick.enboxify(
        """
        here's some text that we
        want to put into a box.
        """,
        hspace=3,
    )
)
output
********************************
*   here's some text that we   *
*   want to put into a box.    *
********************************

items.title: vspace (int)
items.text:
Number of blank lines between the text and the box on the top and bottom. Default is 0.

enboxify() with vspace
print(
    snick.enboxify(
        """
        here's some text that we
        want to put into a box.
        """,
        vspace=1,
    )
)
output
****************************
*                          *
* here's some text that we *
* want to put into a box.  *
*                          *
****************************

items.title: should_strip (bool)
items.text: Passed through to the internal dedent() call. See dedent().

items.title: Conjoiner class
items.text: Conjoiner builds multi-line strings incrementally. You add lines or blocks one at a time and convert to a string at the end.

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
Conjoiner basic usage
from snick import Conjoiner

conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add("First line")
conjoiner.add("Second line")
print(conjoiner)
output
First line
Second line

items.title: Adding multiple parts
items.text:
Pass multiple arguments to add() in a single call:

Conjoiner adding multiple parts
conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add(
    "Line 1",
    "Line 2",
    "Line 3",
)
print(conjoiner)

items.title: Automatic dedenting
items.text:
By default, Conjoiner dedents each part:

Conjoiner with automatic dedenting
conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add(
    """
    This text is indented in the code
    but will be dedented in the output
    """
)
conjoiner.add(
    """
    Same with this text
    it looks nice in the code
    """
)
print(conjoiner)
output
This text is indented in the code
but will be dedented in the output
Same with this text
it looks nice in the code

To preserve indentation, pass should_dedent=False:

Conjoiner preserving indentation
conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add("    Keep this indented", should_dedent=False)

items.title: Adding blank lines
items.text:
Insert blank lines between parts within a single add() call using blanks_between:

Conjoiner with blanks_between
conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add(
    "Section 1",
    "Section 2",
    "Section 3",
    blanks_between=1,
)
print(conjoiner)
output
Section 1

Section 2

Section 3

blanks_between only applies within a single add() call. Use blanks_before and blanks_after to control spacing across calls:

Conjoiner with blanks_before and blanks_after
conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add("first")
conjoiner.add("second", blanks_before=1, blanks_after=1)
conjoiner.add("third")
print(conjoiner)
output
first

second

third

For explicit control, use add_blank() or add_blanks():

Conjoiner with add_blanks()
conjoiner = Conjoiner()
conjoiner.add("first")
conjoiner.add_blanks(2)
conjoiner.add("second")
print(conjoiner)
output
first


second

items.title: Customizing the join string
items.text:
Conjoiner with custom join string
conjoiner = Conjoiner(join_str=" | ")
conjoiner.add("one", "two", "three")
print(conjoiner)
output
one | two | three

items.title: Customizing blank lines
items.text:
Conjoiner with custom blank character
conjoiner = Conjoiner(blank="---")
conjoiner.add("First", "Second", blanks_between=2)
print(conjoiner)
output
First
---
---
Second

items.title: Practical example
items.text:
Building a formatted report:

Conjoiner practical report example
from snick import Conjoiner

def generate_report(title, items, footer):
    conjoiner = Conjoiner()

    conjoiner.add(f"=== {title} ===", blanks_after=1)

    if items:
        conjoiner.add("Items:")
        conjoiner.extend((f"  {i}. {item}" for (i, item) in enumerate(items, 1)), should_dedent=False)
    else:
        conjoiner.add("_No items found._")

    conjoiner.add(f"--- {footer} ---", blanks_before=1)
    return conjoiner

print(generate_report("Daily Report", ["Task A", "Task B", "Task C"], "End of Report"))
output
=== Daily Report ===

Items:
  1. Task A
  2. Task B
  3. Task C

--- End of Report ---

items.title: Conjoiner dataclass
items.text:
Conjoins text parts into a single string.

This is most useful when building multi-line strings where you want to add parts as you go and then produce a final, joined string.
